item.title: Bill Unruh (UBC) — Tue Oct 27, 11:00 AM — MP 1318A
item.description:
Title: Black Holes-- Entropy container or creator
Abstract: The usual model of a black hole is that after it has been created it contains entropy proportional to M^2, (or 1/4 the surface area of the horizon). It is like the cooling off of a hot lump of coal or the emission of radiation by a hot black body radiator. I will argue that a better analogy is an amplifier (like in your radio) for which there is a constant flux of radiation which is created by the amplification process, but which does not have a large internal entropy which slowly leaks out. I will illustrate this by a simple, exactly solvable model of an amplifier and of a 2-D black hole. Host: Anupam Mazumdar
Source: CITA Seminars

item.title: 👻 Ghost Tour of Old Toronto🌙! — Thu Oct 29, 6:30 PM
item.description:
Try New Things in Toronto! # 👻 Ghost Tour of Old Toronto 🌙
### Haunted Hotels, Dark History & The Ghosts of Downtown
Toronto has a long history — and some of it is considerably darker than the history books make it sound.
Join us for an evening walk through **Old Toronto**, where we'll uncover stories of haunted hotels, gruesome executions, mysterious deaths, and some of the stranger legends that have become part of the city's history. We'll walk through the downtown core as the city settles into the evening, stopping along the way for stories about the ghosts, tragedies, and unusual events connected to the streets and buildings around us. And yes, we'll even explore **why Toronto has a long-standing fear of clowns.** 🤡👻
This isn't simply a walk through downtown. It's a **curated storytelling experience** that looks at some of Toronto's history from a decidedly darker perspective.

item.title: Robotics Institute Seminar: Tongjia Zheng, “Scalable Autonomy: From Robot Swarms to Soft Continuum Robots” — Fri Oct 30, 3:00 PM — Myhal Centre for Engineering Innovation & Entrepreneurship
item.description:
Scalable Autonomy: From Robot Swarms to Soft Continuum Robots Join in-person (MY580) or online (Zoom) Abstract My research is motivated by the scalability challenge in autonomous systems. As systems grow in scale—from single robots to large swarms, or from rigid-body mechanisms to infinite-dimensional soft continuum bodies—many traditional methods become impractical. My work addresses this challenge by identifying physics-based, system-level invariances that remain tractable independent of scale, using tools from continuum mechanics, control theory, and applied math.
I will first present a density-based estimation and control framework for robot swarms, inspired by diffusion processes, that drives large robot populations to desired spatial distributions using only local sensing and communication. I will then discuss hydrodynamics-inspired strategies for robot-assisted human evacuation, where a small number of mobile robots guide large crowds through adaptive interaction. Last, I will
